en: The Buddha spoke this Sūtra on the Tathāgata’s Attainment of Enlightenment:
His feet tread upon wheels of a thousand blessings; his body is draped in [robes] and holds a *kamaṇḍalu* flask;
upon his chest, the *svastika* is clearly and distinctly manifest; and from his back, a halo radiates forth, shimmering and overflowing with brilliance.
The lion king’s whiskers curl upward;
he extends his broad and long tongue,
which completely covers the dark and hidden realms.
Its radiance shines boundlessly,
surpassing the brilliance of the sun;
those who behold the Buddha’s light [attain this].
The Tathāgata of Eternal Non-arising and Non-perishing:
he is *p'an* (槃) and thus does not die;
he is *nieh* (涅) and thus is not born.
Stir it and it does not become turbid;
let it settle and it does not become clear;
carry it and it does not become heavy.
It is neither light nor slight;
it is neither dark nor obscure;
it is neither manifest nor bright.
"Name" means not begrudging [one's reputation];
"benefit" means not contending;
"humiliation" means not feeling resentment.
Favored, they do not become arrogant;
dispersed, they do not fall into ruin;
gathered together, they do not act in unison.
High yet not precarious;
low yet level;
flanked yet without companion.
Extensive yet distinct in their formation:
killing is itself non-death;
reviving is itself non-birth.
White hair does not constitute old age,
nor is youth the state of an infant;
when one looks at them, their substance cannot be seen.
Listening to it, one does not hear its sound.
Its great body encompasses the eight directions, filling the empty courtyard;
yet when small, it runs horses within the eye of a needle.
He conceals his form within the dust;
he transforms the ocean into ghee and curd;
he points to the earth as lapis lazuli and crystal.
Grasping the mountain, one immediately knows its weight;
the vast ocean is entirely reduced to a single empty pit;
even a mote of dust can have its number calculated.
The mind knows that all sentient beings,
their celestial palaces and towers, are like a conjured city;
whatever they require is obtained without the need for effortful exertion.
In movement, it is vast and unimpeded;
in stillness, it is profound and unswerving.
With the physical eye, it observes the events of the three periods of time.
Using the five eyes, one constantly dwells together with those who are blind;
there is neither the state of "non-non-intentionality" nor the sentiment of "is-is.
Thus, one transcends the realm of the Three Vehicles.
For those sentient beings who have transgressed beyond the six perfections,
he raises a majestic and fierce cry so that they are not terrified or alarmed.
Grasped, it does not adhere;
looked at, it has form;
it appears and disappears without cause.
The movement subsides of its own accord;
when the eyelids close, it is as if ten thousand *li* away,
and when they open, it comes to rest.
This is that which is neither characteristic nor the characterized,
neither name nor the named;
it is burned yet leaves no ash.
Though submerged, it does not sink;
though the platform is not raised,
and though pressed down, it does not collapse.
One does not rejoice upon finding something lost;
yet one does not weep with sorrow when losing it.
The great assembly does not delight in worldly pleasures.
Alone, one does not linger;
taking up the blade, one cuts without resentment.
Applying medicine, one treats what cannot be cured.
The two minds are of one kind and equal;
they are suddenly and simultaneously distributed,
so that his body reaches every place in its hundreds of millions of manifestations.
The first is named Mida;
the second is named Tathāgata.
When these were praised, the earth shook and thunder resounded from the heavens.
All the followers each have their own place of refuge.
If one has faith, this deity will surely protect them;
if one lacks faith, they will suffer from cold and freezing without clothing.
If one transcribes one fascicle, one’s household will abound in wealth;
if one transcribes two fascicles, one will become intelligent and wise,
and when teaching others to read and recite it, no transverse illnesses shall come.
From within the air, he praised it, saying:
"Inconceivable! This is the Sūtra on the Tathāgata Attaining Enlightenment spoken by the Buddha."
